# Clinical research trials

Volunteers make our game-changing research possible.

We regularly require animals (and sometimes humans!) for our research studies.

See below for current research trials seeking volunteers.

## Dog cancer research trial

University of Queensland veterinary researchers are recruiting pet dogs diagnosed with cancer to test an experimental vaccine.

The clinical research trial is for dogs recently diagnosed with canine appendicular osteosarcoma, a common bone tumour that affects 10,000 dogs a year globally.

Take part in the trial

## Labrador and Golden Retriever overweight research project

University of Queensland veterinary researchers are investigating how obesity and being overweight affects the health and happiness of dogs, focusing on metabolism, gut health, body fat distribution and brain function.

Your participation could help us understand these connections better and help prevent and manage this condition in the future.

Learn more about the study

## Contact us

Contact us if you have a question.

UQ acknowledges the Traditional Owners and their custodianship of the lands on which UQ is situated. Reconciliation at UQ

# Clinical trials

The School of Veterinary Science has several clinical trials and research studies seeking volunteers and input from the public.

Each trial or research study has varying requirements in regards to the assistance the investigators are requiring. We invite you to take a look at the current trials listed below to see if you can contribute.

Please note that all clinical trials and research have animal ethics and/or human ethics approvals, participation is voluntary and any participants can be removed from a trial at any time.

## Dog bone cancer vaccine trial

We are looking for pet dogs diagnosed with cancer to test an experimental vaccine. The clinical research trial is for dogs recently diagnosed with canine appendicular osteosarcoma, a common bone tumour that affects 10,000 dogs a year globally. In this trial, our researchers will assess two vaccine formulations. To be eligible, dogs need to have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma of long bones of the limbs with no evidence of metastasis, or cancer spread, based on a physical exam and radiographs. Dogs can be any breed but must be proceeding to surgery to treat their cancer. Read more about these trials.

Applications for the trial can be made via this webform, or questions can be directed to Dr José Granados Soler (j.granados@uq.edu.au).

## Cattle with lantana camara toxicity

We are looking for cattle that are naturally intoxicated with lantana camara.  Lantana is a common toxic plant in Queensland. We are searching for prognostic indicators of intoxicated cattle to better identify cattle that will survive. If you have cattle that are showing signs of photosensitization and have access to lantana, we would like to include them in the study. Photosensitization will present as thickened or “crusty” skin that is more firm that normal.  It occurs commonly in the white skinned areas, ears, nose and rear legs, but can occur anywhere on the body. Involvement in the study will consist of the cost of the campus vet mileage at $1.81/km roundtrip and the cost of the pharmaceuticals needed to treat.

# Find a clinical trial

Search for a clinical trial in our online registry, or find out about other websites and registries that provide information about clinical trials.

## Search the online registry

Use our search function to start looking for a clinical trial. All clinical trials displayed on this website are sourced from the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ANZCTR). The ANZCTR includes all clinical trials with a recruitment site in Australia that are registered on ANZCTR as well as ClinicalTrials.gov, the US clinical trials registry.

  * Basic search
  * Advanced search

## Other registries

There are other clinical trial registries that provide information on trials in Australia, New Zealand and, in some cases, other countries.

Each site will explain how to search the site for trials by the disease or condition that you are interested in. Some websites also allow you to register your details so you can:

  * receive information on potentially suitable trials when they become available
  * allow researchers to access your information and approach you directly.

### Registry list

The International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) aims to provide a single point of access to information about ongoing and completed clinical trials provided by registries around the world. ANZCTR is one of these registries.

The following Australian websites include listings of clinical trials specific to their 
area of expertise:

  * Australian Cancer Trials
  * Black Dog Institute
  * Cancer Institute NSW
  * GenesisCare
  * Growing Minds Australia
  * Icon Cancer Centre
  * MS Australia Clinical Trials Network
  * Nucleus Network
  * Pulmonary Fibrosis Australasian Clinical Trials Network
  * Victorian Cancer Trials Link (VCTL)

Additional sites providing clinical research information:

  * Australian Lung Foundation
  * Cancer Research Network
  * Cancer Trials Australia
  * Medicines Australia

## Talk to people

You can also find out about clinical trials by talking to a range of people. Learn who you can talk to for information about clinical trials relevant to you.

The problem

## Australia has no way for pet owners to find clinical trials.

In the United States, the AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry, AniTrial, and the Dog Aging Project connect pet owners with hundreds of active studies. Dog and cat owners there can access new cancer immunotherapy, longevity drugs like rapamycin, and novel treatments for kidney disease, epilepsy, and arthritis.

In Australia, clinical research is fragmented across seven veterinary schools with no centralised, owner-accessible registry. Pet owners have no way to discover if a trial relevant to their pet's condition exists. They cannot enrol. Research teams struggle to recruit participants.

PetTrials fixes that. For free.

#### No centralised trial registry

Unlike the US, which has the AVMA registry with hundreds of active studies, Australian pet owners have nowhere to search for trials.

#### Research fragmented across 7 vet schools

UQ, Sydney, Melbourne, Murdoch, CSU, JCU, and Adelaide each run independent studies with no shared recruitment platform.

#### Researchers cannot find participants

Veterinary clinical trials depend on owner participation. Without a matching platform, recruitment is slow and studies are underpowered.

#### Pets miss out on life-saving treatments

Pets with cancer, chronic disease, or age-related conditions could benefit from new therapies, but only if their owners knew the trials existed.

How it works

## Three steps to better care for your pet.

Upload your pet's health records, get matched with relevant studies, and connect directly with research teams. Everything is free for pet owners.

Step 01

### Upload

Upload your dog or cat's vaccination records, diagnoses, medications, surgical history, and vet visit notes. Build a complete longitudinal health profile that grows with your pet. Completely free.

Step 02

### Match

Our matching engine compares your pet's profile against active clinical trials at Australian universities and research institutions. When a relevant study opens, you are notified immediately.

Step 03

### Connect

Review study details, eligibility, and what participation involves. PetTrials arranges introductions with research teams and guides you through informed consent and enrolment.

Research areas

## Active and emerging trial areas.

Australian veterinary schools run research across a growing range of conditions. These are the therapeutic areas where trials are most active or expected to recruit.

#### Cancer

Osteosarcoma, lymphoma, mast cell tumours, hemangiosarcoma, immunotherapy, CAR-T.

#### Heart disease

Cardiomyopathy, valve disease, rapamycin studies, heart failure management.

#### Kidney disease

Chronic kidney disease, novel therapeutics, dietary interventions.

#### Neurology

Epilepsy, degenerative myelopathy, cognitive decline, seizure management.

#### Gastrointestinal

Chronic enteropathy, inflammatory bowel disease, microbiome therapies.

#### Orthopaedics

Osteoarthritis, joint disease, pain management, regenerative medicine.

#### Dermatology

Atopic dermatitis, pyoderma, novel topical therapies, allergy management.

#### Ageing & longevity

Rapamycin, lifespan extension, age-related disease prevention, biological ageing.

### Why join a clinical trial?

  * Access novel treatments not yet available at regular vets
  * Free or subsidised veterinary care during the study
  * Close monitoring by specialist veterinary researchers
  * Contribute to research that helps all animals, and humans too
  * Your pet's full health profile in one secure place
  * Withdraw at any time. Participation is always voluntary

For pet owners

## Your pet's health history, in one place.

Even if there is no trial available for your pet right now, PetTrials gives you something no other Australian platform offers: a centralised, secure digital health record for your dog or cat.

Upload vaccinations, diagnoses, medications, and surgical history. Track changes over time. Share your profile with any vet. And when a trial does open that matches your pet's condition, you will be the first to know.

Think of it as a health passport for your pet, built for the future of veterinary medicine.

For researchers

## Recruit faster. Enrol smarter.

Veterinary clinical trials depend on finding the right animals with the right conditions. PetTrials gives research teams access to a growing database of pet health profiles, pre-screened and ready for eligibility matching.

List your trial on PetTrials for free. Reach pet owners who are actively looking for research opportunities. Reduce recruitment timelines and improve enrolment rates.

List your trial

#### Pre-screened profiles

Owners upload detailed vet histories including diagnoses, medications, and procedures, enabling rapid eligibility assessment.

#### Targeted recruitment

When you list a trial, PetTrials notifies owners whose pets match your inclusion criteria. No more passive waiting for referrals.

#### Recruitment analytics

Track views, enquiries, and enrolment rates for your listed studies through the PetTrials research dashboard.

#### Free to list

Listing trials on PetTrials is free for Australian veterinary schools and research institutions. Always.

About us

## Built by scientists. Driven by purpose.

PetTrials is a division of Altered Carbon Synthetic Biology Pty Ltd (ACN 649 555 993), an Australian synthetic biology company.

PetTrials was created to connect pet owners and veterinary researchers, so that emerging treatments can reach the animals that need them through well-recruited clinical trials.

PetTrials draws on expertise in molecular biology, clinical trial management, computational biology, and veterinary science, with a commitment to advancing companion animal health through rigorous research.

#### Dr Matthew Latif, PhD

Chief Scientific Officer. Over 25 years in R&D commercialisation. PhD from the University of Queensland. Winner of the H&M Global Change Award (2022) and the 2025 Australian National Science Week Award.

#### Proven track record

Our team has collectively secured over USD $227 million in competitive grant funding and brings experience across protein engineering, clinical research, regulatory compliance, and research translation.

#### Australian-operated, Australian-stored

All pet health data is stored securely in Australia under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and the Australian Privacy Principles. Your information is only used for trial matching.

FAQ

## Common questions.

Is PetTrials really free for pet owners? +

Yes. Uploading your pet's vet history, receiving trial match notifications, and connecting with research teams costs nothing. PetTrials is funded by Altered Carbon Synthetic Biology and by research partnerships.

What information do I need to upload? +

As much as you have: vaccination records, diagnoses, medications, surgical history, vet visit notes. The more complete your profile, the better we can match you with relevant trials.

Is it safe to join a clinical trial? +

All veterinary clinical trials at Australian institutions are reviewed by Animal Ethics Committees (AECs) under the Australian Code for the Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes. Your pet's welfare is the top priority.

Can I withdraw my pet from a trial? +

Absolutely. Participation is always voluntary and you can withdraw at any stage. Informed consent is required before enrolment and is not a binding contract.

What if there is no trial for my pet right now? +

Your profile stays active. When a new study opens that matches your pet's condition, breed, or age, you will be notified automatically. New trials are listed regularly.

Is this only for dogs? +

PetTrials launched with a focus on dogs, since they represent the largest clinical trial population. Cat trials are already listed and the cat profile flow is being added as the platform grows.

What happens to my pet's data? +

Your data is stored securely in Australia under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). It is only used for trial matching and is never shared with third parties without your explicit consent. See our Privacy Policy.

I am a researcher: how do I list a trial? +

Contact us using the details below. Listing is free for all Australian veterinary schools and research institutions.

# Clinical Trials for Dogs with Cancer

Links last verified: August 20, 2026

## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology

When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.

Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.

These may include: 

  * A dog’s breed
  * Age
  * Weight
  * Overall health
  * Life expectancy
  * Cancer type
  * Cancer stage
  * Previous care
  * ...and other medical factors

Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.

It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.

Research funding may cover only certain tests, medications, procedures, or appointments. 
PetCure Oncology provides stereotactic radiation surgery and stereotactic radiation therapy, commonly known as SRS and SRT. These highly precise forms of radiation therapy have been used in human oncology and are now available for dogs with certain types of cancer.

PetCure Oncology reports using SRS and SRT in thousands of companion animals with a variety of tumor types. Its affiliated veterinary specialists continue to study these approaches to better understand their potential benefits, safety considerations, side effects, and appropriate applications in canine cancer care.

## Keep in Mind

Clinical trials may explore new approaches to diagnosing or supporting dogs with cancer. These may include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical procedures, temperature-based therapies, immunotherapy, photodynamic therapy, and other emerging approaches.

Although many clinical trials take place at veterinary colleges and teaching hospitals, a growing number of specialty and referral practices also participate in canine cancer research. Some studies require every appointment to be completed at the participating institution, while others may allow certain tests, procedures, or follow-up visits to be handled by a dog’s regular veterinary team.

The words “experimental” and “investigational” can understandably feel concerning. Before a new therapy or procedure reaches a veterinary clinical trial, researchers have typically completed earlier stages of evaluation. However, unknowns may remain regarding its safety, effectiveness, or potential side effects. A study is offered because researchers believe the approach may provide meaningful benefits, but participation does not guarantee a positive outcome.

Pet parents should review the study’s purpose, requirements, possible benefits, known and unknown risks, costs, and available alternatives with the clinical trial team and their dog’s veterinary care provider before making a decision.

# Welcome to K9MD

It is widely acknowledged that early detection greatly enhances the chance of a patient's survival. K9 Medical Detection NZ aims to increase the rate of early detection.

 K9 Medical Detection New Zealand Charitable Trust's mission is to improve the health of all New Zealander's by using specially trained dogs working in a controlled clinical environment to assist in the detection of cancer and other diseases. To create a simple diagnostic urine test as a value added tool in the fight against cancer.

## What We Do

K9MD is dedicated to advancing medical detection capabilities through the unique and highly effective use of trained canines. Our mission is to improve health outcomes and enhance quality of life by harnessing the extraordinary olfactory abilities of dogs to detect diseases early and accurately.

## How You Can Help

Your assistance is greatly appreciated. Your donation will support the welfare and training of K9 Medical Detection NZ's dedicated team of dogs.

## Our Dogs

K9MD dogs love going to work. 
I fully support Pauline and her team and hope for the sake of all New Zealanders that this becomes a form of early detection for cancer in the future.

# Comparative Oncology (Canine Trials and Resources)

Image: A physician and assistant examine a dog patient at the University of Minnesota

Credit: University of Minnesota

As in humans, cancers in pet dogs arise spontaneously. Dogs also have similar genomes, immune responses, living environment, and tumor complexity to humans. Studying pet dogs in cancer research, including in clinical trials, can provide valuable information for the development of future treatments for people.

The Integrated Canine Data Commons

The Integrated Canine Data Commons (ICDC) is a node in the larger NCI human Cancer Research Data Commons (CRDC). The Division of Cancer Treatment and Diagnosis (DCTD) developed the publicly available and searchable ICDC to incorporate genomic, proteomic, imaging, clinical trial, biomarker, population study, cancer model, and immuno-oncology data. This enables comparative analysis with tumors that arise spontaneously in pet dogs and advances research on human cancers.

PRECINCT Research Network: PRE-medical Cancer Immunotherapy Network Canine Trials 

In 2017, NCI granted five teams U01 awards (RFA-CA-17-001) and one team a U24 award (RFA-CA-17-002) to perform canine immunotherapy trials and correlative analyses. In 2022, the program was renewed with U01 awards (RFA-CA-21-050) issued to five new universities and a U24 award issued to the same team as in 2017 (RFA-CA-21-051).

Immuno-oncology Canine Clinical Trials

DCTD is developing novel immuno-oncology agents for use in clinical trials involving pet dogs with cancer to inform, optimize, and better understand the underlying biology and administration of these agents in human patients. These canine-specific reagents target promising immune regulatory proteins. They will be useful not only as therapeutics, both as monotherapies and in combination with other cancer treatments, but also for pharmacodynamic assays and as imaging agents.

This multi-year, multi-phase, coordinated project is a collaboration between DCTD and the NCI Center for Cancer Research Comparative Oncology Program (COP). It leverages the COP’s veterinary clinical trial infrastructure (Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium) to advance the DCTD canine drug development pipeline. Newly developed agents will ultimately be shared with the extramural comparative oncology community to further cancer research.

Longitudinal Studies in Dogs with Cancer

The purpose of these studies is to obtain longitudinal tumor specimens that can be analyzed to inform our understanding of the molecular basis of canine cancer progression. In addition, this work will help determine whether pet dogs are a reliable model for evaluating the effectiveness of investigational therapeutics and treatment regimens for potential future use in humans.

Goals

  * Expand molecular studies to understand treatment and resistance throughout the development and evolution of malignant disease using pet dogs as a model

Objectives

  * To longitudinally track individual dogs that may receive treatments and/or participate in clinical trials or receive no treatment at the request of the owner (to study the natural history of the cancer in molecular detail)
  * To collect annotated canine cancer patient clinical/trial history and molecular characterization of biopsy material and blood at time of diagnosis, post-treatment, and at relapse. These will be used to to determine whether and in what circumstances naturally occurring tumors arise in dogs. They are good models of human cancer, tumor response, development of resistance to therapeutic regimens, and disease progression
